knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true"), collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)

bayescompR runs Stan programs in R. This vignette walks through the full
workflow on the eight schools model: writing the program, binding data,
sampling, checking convergence and using the draws.

```{r}
library(bayescompR)
```

## A Stan program

The model is the non centered eight schools model of Rubin (1981) and
Gelman et al. (2013). Each school has an estimated treatment effect `y` with
standard error `sigma`; the true effects `theta` share a normal population
distribution.

```{r}
code <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> J;
  array[J] real y;
  array[J] real<lower=0> sigma;
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> tau;
  vector[J] eta;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[J] theta = mu + tau * eta;
}
model {
  mu ~ normal(0, 5);
  tau ~ cauchy(0, 5);
  eta ~ std_normal();
  y ~ normal(theta, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
  array[J] real y_rep = normal_rng(theta, sigma);
}
"
schools <- list(J = 8, y = c(28, 8, -3, 7, -1, 1, 18, 12),
                sigma = c(15, 10, 16, 11, 9, 11, 10, 18))
```

`bayescomp_check()` parses and type checks a program without data, which is
useful while writing a model.

```{r}
bayescomp_check(code)
```

## Compiling and binding data

`bayescomp_model()` compiles the program into R closures, reads and
validates the data against the `data` block, and runs `transformed data`.

```{r}
model <- bayescomp_model(code, data = schools)
model
```

Data are checked against their declarations, and the error names the
offending variable:

```{r, error = TRUE}
bad <- schools
bad$sigma[3] <- -1
bayescomp_model(code, data = bad)
```

## Sampling

`bayescomp_sample()` runs the No-U-Turn sampler with Stan's adaptation.
Each chain gets its own random number stream derived from `seed`, so the
results are reproducible and do not depend on `cores`. Chains run
sequentially unless you pass `cores` or set `options(mc.cores = 4)` (see
`vignette("performance")`). Short chains keep
this vignette fast; use the defaults (1000 warmup and 1000 sampling
iterations) for real analyses.

```{r}
fit <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 4, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 300,
                        seed = 2024, refresh = 0)
fit
```

The summary reports the posterior mean, median, standard deviation, median
absolute deviation, 5% and 95% quantiles, rank normalized R-hat, and bulk
and tail effective sample sizes.

```{r}
summary(fit, c("mu", "tau", "theta"))
```

## Diagnostics

```{r}
bayescomp_diagnose(fit)
```

R-hat below 1.01 and effective sample sizes above about 400 indicate that
the chains agree and the estimates are precise enough for most purposes.
Divergent transitions suggest geometry the sampler cannot explore reliably;
see `vignette("diagnostics")`.

```{r}
plot(fit, c("mu", "tau"))
```

## Using the draws

```{r}
draws <- bayescomp_draws(fit, c("mu", "tau"), format = "matrix")
dim(draws)
theta <- bayescomp_extract(fit, "theta")  # draws by schools
dim(theta)
colMeans(theta)
```

Posterior predictive checks use the generated quantities:

```{r}
y_rep <- bayescomp_extract(fit, "y_rep")
mean(apply(y_rep, 1, max) >= max(schools$y))
```

With the posterior package installed, `bayescomp_as_draws()` converts a fit
to a `draws_array` for use with posterior, bayesplot and loo.

## Faster approximations

Optimization, Laplace approximation, Pathfinder and ADVI are much cheaper
than sampling. Pathfinder is also a good way to initialize chains.

```{r}
pf <- bayescomp_pathfinder(model, seed = 1)
summary(pf, c("mu", "tau"))
fit2 <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 200, iter_sampling = 200,
                         init = pf, seed = 3, refresh = 0)
```

Pathfinder warns when the Pareto k diagnostic of its importance weights
exceeds 0.7. Hierarchical models such as this one often trigger it: the
normal approximation is then not reliable as a posterior, but its draws are
still useful starting points for MCMC. `vignette("inference")` compares
all the algorithms.

## The model interface

The log density, its gradient and the parameter transforms are available
directly, for use with other software:

```{r}
u <- rep(0.1, bayescomp_dim(model))
bayescomp_log_prob(model, u)
head(bayescomp_grad_log_prob(model, u))
str(bayescomp_constrain(model, u)[c("mu", "tau")])
```
